description: Hinge and ball-and-socket joints, articulating bones and the types of movement they allow.
content_html:
What Is a Synovial Joint?

Every freely movable joint in the body — at the shoulder, elbow, hip and knee — is a synovial joint. Synovial joints are the most common type of joint in the body, and they all share the same basic structure: a capsule surrounding the joint, fluid inside to reduce friction, and a range of soft-tissue structures that hold the joint together and prevent injury. Understanding these structures is important not just for anatomy, but for explaining how joints withstand the demands of sport.

Structures of a Synovial Joint

The outer shell of a synovial joint is the joint capsule. It is made of tough, fibrous connective tissue that wraps completely around the joint, holding the bones in position and containing the joint fluid. Inside the capsule, the synovial membrane lines the inner surface and produces synovial fluid — a viscous substance that coats the ends of the bones inside the joint, dramatically reducing friction and allowing bones to glide smoothly past each other. During the warm-up phase of exercise, synovial fluid becomes less viscous and spreads more effectively, which is one reason why warming up reduces injury risk.

Covering the ends of the bones inside the joint is articular cartilage, a smooth tissue that absorbs compressive forces and provides an almost frictionless surface. Ligaments are short, tough bands of fibrous tissue that connect bone to bone across the joint — the primary restraints against excessive movement. Tendons connect muscles to bone, transmitting contractile force to the skeleton to produce movement at the joint.

Key Fact

The four key components of a synovial joint: synovial fluid (lubricates and reduces friction between bone surfaces), articular cartilage (absorbs compression, provides frictionless surface), ligaments (connect bone to bone, prevent excessive movement), tendons (connect muscle to bone, transmit force for movement).

Types of Synovial Joint

OCR identifies two types of synovial joint and four specific joints that are directly examined. A hinge joint permits movement in one plane only — flexion and extension. The knee (femur articulating with the tibia) and the elbow (humerus articulating with the radius and ulna) are both hinge joints. A ball-and-socket joint permits movement in multiple planes. The shoulder (head of the humerus fitting into the socket of the scapula) and the hip (head of the femur fitting into the socket of the pelvis) are ball-and-socket joints.

Articulating Bones at Each Joint

The OCR specification requires you to name the articulating bones at all four joints. At the knee, the femur (thigh bone) articulates with the tibia (shin bone) — these two long bones form the hinge. At the elbow, the humerus articulates with both the radius and the ulna — three bones meet here, which is why the elbow allows both hinge movement (flexion/extension) and some rotation. At the shoulder, the humerus articulates with the scapula — the rounded head of the humerus sits in the shallow socket of the scapula, enabling the greatest range of movement in the body. At the hip, the femur articulates with the pelvis — the rounded head of the femur slots into the deep cup of the pelvis, creating a stable but mobile ball-and-socket joint.

Key Fact

Knee: femur + tibia (hinge). Elbow: humerus + radius + ulna (hinge). Shoulder: humerus + scapula (ball-and-socket). Hip: femur + pelvis (ball-and-socket). These are the four joints on the OCR specification — learn the articulating bones for each.

Types of Movement at Joints

Flexion is a decrease in the angle at a joint — bending. Extension is an increase in the angle — straightening. Both occur at all four OCR joints. At the elbow and knee (hinge joints), flexion and extension are the only movements possible because the structure of the joint restricts movement to a single plane.

At the shoulder and hip (ball-and-socket joints), a much wider range of movements is available. Abduction is movement of a limb away from the midline — lifting the arm out to the side in a star jump. Adduction is movement towards the midline — bringing the arm back down. Both abduction and adduction are available at the shoulder and hip but not at the elbow or knee.

Rotation of the shoulder is turning the arm in or out along its long axis. A cricket bowler’s arm rotates at the shoulder during delivery. Circumduction of the shoulder is a circular movement combining flexion, abduction, extension and adduction in sequence — the arm traces a full cone shape. Throwing a javelin involves circumduction of the shoulder.

A 4-mark exam question might ask how the structures of a synovial joint help prevent injury during sport. A well-developed answer links each structure to its protective role: ligaments prevent bones from moving too far out of alignment (stabilising the knee in a tackle); articular cartilage absorbs impact forces when landing from a jump; synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces the wear on cartilage surfaces during sustained aerobic exercise. Always name the structure, state what it does, and give a sporting example.

As body temperature rises during a warm-up, synovial fluid becomes less viscous and distributes more evenly across the joint surfaces. This increases the range of movement available and reduces friction, meaning joints can work more efficiently. Ligaments and tendons also become more pliable at higher temperatures, reducing the risk of tears. This is the physiological reason why a warm-up includes a pulse raiser and stretching before high-intensity work.
exam_tip_html: On a ‘State Two’ question about synovial joint structures, give two genuinely different structures — do not write two answers that describe the same component. Spread your answers: one structural component (e.g. ligaments) and one lubricating component (e.g. synovial fluid) will demonstrate wider knowledge. On a 4-mark ‘Explain’ question about movement types, state the movement, define it (angle increasing/decreasing, towards/away from midline), name the joint where it occurs, and give a sporting example — that covers all four marks. When naming articulating bones, state all the bones at a joint: the elbow has three articulating bones (humerus, radius and ulna) — writing only two loses a mark. OCR does not require plantar flexion or dorsiflexion in this section — the four named joints and their standard movement types are the focus.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Synovial joints share four key components: synovial fluid (reduces friction), articular cartilage (absorbs compression), ligaments (bone to bone, prevent excessive movement) and tendons (muscle to bone, transmit force) — each can be linked to injury prevention in sport.
  • The four OCR joints with their articulating bones: knee (femur + tibia, hinge), elbow (humerus + radius + ulna, hinge), shoulder (humerus + scapula, ball-and-socket), hip (femur + pelvis, ball-and-socket).
  • Ball-and-socket joints (shoulder and hip) allow flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction. Hinge joints (elbow, knee) allow flexion and extension only.

practice_questions.text: Name the two bones that articulate at the hip joint.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: femur and pelvis (both required for the mark).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'ligament' and state its role in a synovial joint.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining a ligament as a strong, elastic connective tissue; 1 mark for stating it connects bone to bone across a joint to provide stability and limit excessive movement.

practice_questions.text: Describe the role of synovial fluid in a joint and explain how a warm-up improves its effectiveness.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for stating that synovial fluid lubricates the joint and reduces friction between the articulating surfaces; 1 mark for stating that it nourishes the articular cartilage; 1 mark for explaining that during a warm-up, rising body temperature makes synovial fluid less viscous, allowing it to distribute more evenly and improving range of movement / reducing injury risk.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the shoulder joint allows a greater range of movement than the elbow joint, referring to joint type and the articulating bones at each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying the shoulder as a ball-and-socket joint; 1 mark for explaining that the rounded head of the humerus fits into the socket of the scapula, allowing movement in all planes (flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, circumduction); 1 mark for identifying the elbow as a hinge joint; 1 mark for explaining that the shape of the joint (humerus articulating with radius and ulna) restricts movement to flexion and extension in a single plane only.

practice_questions.text: State two types of movement that are available at a ball-and-socket joint but NOT at a hinge joint.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of any two correct movements available at ball-and-socket joints only: abduction (moving a limb away from the midline), adduction (moving a limb towards the midline), rotation (turning the limb along its long axis), circumduction (circular movement combining flexion, abduction, extension and adduction). Two near-identical answers (e.g. abduction and adduction described in the same way) are awarded 1 mark only.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old county-level swimmer performs repeated overhead arm strokes during training. Analyse how the structures of the shoulder synovial joint support performance and reduce injury risk during this activity.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: At least two structures discussed in detail with accurate physiological explanation; each structure linked specifically to the demands of overhead swimming (e.g. synovial fluid becoming less viscous during warm-up to allow the full range of circumduction required; ligaments stabilising the ball-and-socket joint against the repetitive shoulder rotation forces; articular cartilage absorbing compressive forces during the pull-through); technically accurate language throughout.

Secure: Two structures identified and mostly accurately explained; applied to swimming in general terms; link between structure and performance present.

Developing: One or two structures named with limited explanation; sporting application vague.

Emerging: Basic naming of structures; little explanation of function or sporting application.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of joint is found at the hip and shoulder?
What is the function of synovial fluid in a joint?
options: To connect bone to bone and prevent dislocation
To absorb compressive forces during landing
To lubricate the joint surfaces and reduce friction
To produce red blood cells for oxygen delivery

knowledge_checks.q: At the elbow, the humerus articulates with the radius and the _____.
Moving a limb away from the midline of the body is called _____.
Match each joint to its articulating bones:

flashcard_questions.a: A freely movable joint enclosed in a capsule and lubricated by synovial fluid, allowing a range of movement between two bones.

flashcard_questions.q: What do ligaments connect, and why is this important in sport?
flashcard_questions.a: Bone to bone across a joint, providing stability and limiting excessive movement that could cause injury.

flashcard_questions.q: Name the two types of synovial joint assessed in OCR PE.
What type of synovial joint is the elbow, and which bones form it?
flashcard_questions.a: Hinge joint formed by the humerus, radius and ulna, allowing flexion and extension only.

flashcard_questions.q: Which joints in the body are ball-and-socket joints?
flashcard_questions.a: Shoulder (humerus and scapula) and hip (femur and pelvis).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between abduction and adduction?
flashcard_questions.a: Abduction moves a limb away from the midline; adduction moves it towards the midline.

flashcard_questions.q: What is circumduction of the shoulder?
flashcard_questions.a: A circular movement in which the arm traces a full cone shape, available only at ball-and-socket joints such as the shoulder and hip.

flashcard_questions.q: Why does warming up improve synovial joint function?
flashcard_questions.a: Rising temperature makes synovial fluid less viscous, spreading more effectively and reducing friction.

flashcard_questions.q: What movement types are available at a hinge joint?
flashcard_questions.a: Flexion and extension only — movement is restricted to one plane by the joint structure.

flashcard_questions.q: What is articular cartilage and what does it do?
flashcard_questions.a: Smooth tissue covering bone ends inside a joint; absorbs compressive forces and provides a frictionless surface.

flashcard_questions.q: State the articulating bones at the knee joint and the type of joint it is.
flashcard_questions.a: Femur and tibia form the knee — a hinge joint allowing flexion and extension.
Decreasing the angle at a joint, bending the limb segment closer to the body.

glossary_terms.definition: A freely movable joint enclosed in a capsule and lubricated by synovial fluid, allowing a range of movement between two bones.
The fibrous outer sleeve that encloses a synovial joint, holding the two bones together and keeping synovial fluid in.
The thick, slippery fluid inside a synovial joint that reduces friction between the articulating surfaces and nourishes the cartilage.
Strong, elastic connective tissues that connect bone to bone across a joint, providing stability and limiting excessive movement.
Strong, fibrous cords that connect muscle to bone, transmitting the force of muscular contraction to produce movement.
A joint that allows movement in one plane only (flexion and extension), like a door hinge.
A joint where the rounded head of one bone fits into the cup-shaped socket of another, allowing movement in all planes.
Decreasing the angle at a joint, moving the limb segment closer to the body.
Increasing the angle at a joint, straightening the limb.
Moving a limb away from the midline of the body.
Moving a limb towards the midline of the body.

hero_image_caption: Synovial joints at the knee, elbow, shoulder and hip are the four joints assessed in OCR PE.
narration_script: Every freely movable joint in the body is a synovial joint. These joints share a common structure: a joint capsule enclosing the joint, synovial fluid to reduce friction, articular cartilage to absorb compressive forces, ligaments connecting bone to bone for stability, and tendons transmitting muscle force to bone. OCR specifies four joints you must know in detail. The knee is a hinge joint formed by the femur and tibia, allowing only flexion and extension. The elbow is also a hinge joint, formed by the humerus, radius and ulna. The shoulder is a ball-and-socket joint, formed by the humerus and scapula, allowing the greatest range of movement in the body. The hip is also a ball-and-socket joint, formed by the femur and pelvis. Ball-and-socket joints allow flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation and circumduction. Hinge joints allow flexion and extension only. Remember: abduction moves a limb away from the midline; adduction brings it back. During a warm-up, synovial fluid becomes less viscous, improving its lubricating effect and reducing injury risk.
